narr: In this section, we'll explore the rules for talking about quantities and numbers in English, which is essential for engineering communication.
Let's start with how to express different amounts of things.

data.heading: Expressing Large Quantities
bullets: We use 'a lot' when there is no noun
Much/many are normally used in negatives and questions
'A lot of' can also be used in place of much/many
We use 'plenty of' in affirmatives to mean more than enough

narr: When we want to talk about large quantities, English has several expressions depending on context.
First, we use 'a lot' when there's no noun following it, as in 'James eats a lot'.
For questions and negative statements, we typically use 'much' with uncountable nouns and 'many' with countable nouns, like 'Do you have many friends?' or 'Don't eat much chocolate'.
However, 'a lot of' can also be used in these situations, making it more versatile.
In positive statements, 'plenty of' indicates more than enough, as in 'We have plenty of time'.

data.heading: Small Quantities
bullets: We use 'little' + uncountable nouns
We use 'few' + plural countable nouns
'A little' and 'a few' mean some, but not a lot
'Very little' and 'very few' mean not much/many
Comparative forms: 'less' and 'fewer'

narr: When discussing small quantities, English has specific expressions.
We use 'little' before uncountable nouns, like 'I have very little time'.
For plural countable nouns, we use 'few', as in 'The town only has a few cinemas'.
'A little' and 'a few' indicate some quantity, but not much or many.
When we want to emphasize scarcity, we use 'very little' and 'very few'.
For comparisons, we use 'less' with uncountable nouns and 'fewer' with countable nouns.

data.heading: More or Less Than You Need
bullets: Too + adjective/adverb
Too much + uncountable nouns
Too many + plural countable nouns
(Not) enough + noun
(Not) enough + adjective/adverb

narr: When we have more or less than we need, English has specific constructions.
We use 'too' before adjectives or adverbs to indicate excess, like 'It's too big' or 'You're speaking too quietly'.
For uncountable nouns, we use 'too much', as in 'There's too much traffic'.
For plural countable nouns, we use 'too many', like 'There are too many tourists'.
When we don't have enough, we use 'enough' before a noun, such as 'not enough eggs'.
'Enough' can also follow adjectives or adverbs, like 'It isn't big enough' or 'You aren't walking fast enough'.

data.heading: Zero Quantity
bullets: Any + uncountable or plural noun with negative verb
No + uncountable or plural noun with affirmative verb
None (without a noun) in short answers

narr: To express zero quantity, English has three main constructions.
With negative verbs, we use 'any' with uncountable or plural nouns, like 'There isn't any milk'.
With affirmative verbs, we use 'no' with uncountable or plural nouns, as in 'There's no milk'.
In short answers, we use 'none' without a following noun, like 'How many eggs do we have?' 'None.'
Now let's move on to discussing numbers, which is crucial for engineering contexts.
We'll cover types of numbers, working with numbers, and describing proportions and averages.

data.heading: Types of Numbers
bullets: Odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7...
Even numbers: 2, 4, 6, 8...
Prime numbers: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11...
Approximate numbers (roughly correct)
Discrete numbers (separate, cannot be divided)
Aggregate (total of a set of numbers)
Random number (chosen by chance)

narr: In mathematics and engineering, we work with different types of numbers.
Odd numbers are integers not divisible by 2: 1, 3, 5, 7 and so on.
Even numbers are integers divisible by 2: 2, 4, 6, 8 and so on.
Prime numbers are numbers that cannot be divided by any other number except themselves and 1: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 and so on.
An approximate number is roughly correct but not precise.
A discrete number or unit is separate and cannot be divided into smaller units of the same thing.
An aggregate is a number reached by totaling a set of numbers.
A random number is one chosen by chance, meaning you cannot predict it.

data.heading: Working with Numbers
bullets: Calculate: to determine a number precisely
Estimate: to make a rough guess at a number
Round up/down: to make a number into the nearest whole number
Total: to add up a set of numbers
Tally: to match or agree
Deduct: to take away or subtract
Values: individual numbers in a set of data

narr: To calculate means to determine a number precisely.
To estimate means to make a rough guess at a number.
Rounding up or down means making a number into the nearest whole number.
To total means to add up a set of numbers.
When figures tally, they match or agree.
To deduct means to take away or subtract one number from another.
Values are individual numbers in a set of data.
When working with numbers, there are several operations and terms to be familiar with.

data.heading: Working with Numbers (cont.)
bullets: Variables: characteristics that can take on different values
Incidence: how frequently something occurs
Magnitude: the size of something
Estimate: to make a rough guess
Area: approximately the same
Workings: all calculations leading up to an answer

narr: Variables are characteristics that can take on different values.
Incidence refers to how frequently something occurs.
Magnitude simply refers to the size of something.
When making calculations, it's good to make an estimate first.
The area refers to being approximately the same.
Workings are all the calculations leading up to an answer.

data.heading: Describing Proportions
bullets: The majority (56%) of those questioned
The highest percentage of smokers
The highest proportion of smokers
Only two per cent of the US population
This small fraction of the population
Only a small minority of US workers (around 5%)

narr: When describing parts of a whole in academic texts, we use various expressions.
We can refer to 'the majority' followed by a percentage, like 'the majority of those questioned'.
We can use 'the highest percentage' to describe a portion, as in 'the highest percentage of smokers'.
Similarly, we can use 'the highest proportion' of a group.
We can specify exact percentages with 'per cent', like 'two per cent of the US population'.
We can refer to 'a small fraction' of a population.
We can also mention 'a small minority' with an approximate percentage.

data.heading: Talking About Averages
bullets: The mean is obtained by calculating the total of all data values
Then dividing by the number of data values
Formula: mean = total of all data values ÷ number of data values

narr: When looking at data, it's useful to know about averages, specifically the mean.
The mean is obtained by calculating the total of all the data values.
Then you divide that total by the number of data values.
In formula terms, it's expressed as mean equals total of all data values divided by the number of data values.

data.heading: Problem 1 — Power Cut Scenario
data.problem: Imagine there was a power cut in your house. What would you find it most frustrating not to be able to do?
data.result: Personal answers will vary depending on individual circumstances and priorities

narr: Let's consider the first listening comprehension question.
This question asks you to imagine a power cut in your house.
You need to identify what you would find most frustrating not to be able to do.
To answer this, consider your essential daily activities that depend on electricity.
Think about how technology affects your daily routine.
Consider how you communicate with others and what devices you need for that.
Also reflect on comfort aspects like lighting, heating, or cooling.
The answer will vary for each person based on their individual circumstances and priorities.

data.problem: Listen again. What things couldn't Chris do during his day without power? Make notes for each of these times: (1) 7 a.m. - 9 a.m.; (2) 9 a.m. – midday; (3) midday - 2 p.m.; (4) 2 p.m. - 6 p.m.; (5) 6 p.m. onwards.

Listen for activities mentioned in each period

narr: The third question requires more detailed listening as you need to identify specific activities Chris couldn't do during different time periods.
First, divide the day into the five specified time periods.
As you listen again, pay close attention to activities mentioned in each period.
Note which of these activities required electricity and therefore couldn't be done.
Organize your findings by time period to create a comprehensive list.
This will help you understand the impact of power loss throughout the day.

data.heading: Problem 4 — Vocabulary in Context
data.problem: Read some of the expressions Chris uses. What do the bold verb phrases mean? (1) I read the news on my tablet and the battery life drops from 65% to 55% in a few minutes. (2) Skype calls really drain the power. (3) I close down unnecessary programs and turn the brightness of my screen down to its lowest level. (4) Finally,

Consider the context in which each phrase is used
Determine the meaning based on the surrounding text

data.result: Explanation of each bold verb phrase in context

narr: The fourth question focuses on vocabulary in context, specifically verb phrases related to power usage.
For each sentence, identify the bold verb phrase and consider how it's used.
Think about what action is being described and how it relates to power consumption.
The first phrase describes battery life decreasing quickly, indicating rapid power usage.
The second phrase suggests that Skype calls consume a lot of power.
The third phrase describes actions taken to reduce power consumption.
Understanding these phrases helps with discussing technology and power usage.
